prompt: At a small company, nine employees each earn about $\$40{,}000$ and the owner earns $\$400{,}000$. Which statement about the ten salaries is true?

choices.label: The mean is greater than the median
The mean is less than the median
The mean and the median are equal

hint: The median only cares about the MIDDLE value. The mean adds up every dollar, including the owner's.

hints.text: The median only cares about the MIDDLE value. The mean adds up every dollar, including the owner's.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Warm up with $1, 1, 1, 100$. Median $= 1$. Mean $= \frac{103}{4} = 25.75$. One huge value drags the mean up but leaves the median alone. Same idea here.
The median of ten salaries is the average of the 5th and 6th values, both about $\$40{,}000$. Now compute the mean: $\frac{9(40{,}000) + 400{,}000}{10}$.
Mean $= \frac{760{,}000}{10} = \$76{,}000$, median $\approx \$40{,}000$. The mean is greater: choice A.

explanation: Sorted, the salaries are nine values near $\$40{,}000$ and one at $\$400{,}000$. The 5th and 6th values are both about $\$40{,}000$, so the median is about $\$40{,}000$.
The mean uses every dollar: $\frac{9 \times 40{,}000 + 400{,}000}{10} = \frac{760{,}000}{10}$, which is $\$76{,}000$.
The one huge salary pulls the mean far above the median, so choice A is true. (Choice D mixes up the two: $\$76{,}000$ is the mean.)

alternativeExplanations.title: Shape tells the story
steps: Nine salaries pile up on the left and one sits far to the right: skewed right.
In a right-skewed distribution the mean is pulled toward the tail, so mean $>$ median.
That matches choice A without computing a thing.

alternativeExplanations.title: The trap in choice D
steps: $\$76{,}000$ is a real number from this problem, which makes D tempting.
But it is the MEAN. Nobody at the company earns anywhere near $\$76{,}000$, which is exactly why the median is the better "typical salary" here.
The median stays at about $\$40{,}000$, so D is false and A is true.
